title: Λύκος καὶ Ποιμήν
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 229. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Λύκος ἀκολουθῶν ποίμνῃ προβάτων οὐδὲν ἠδίκει.
sentences.tr: Lykos akolouthōn poimnēi probatōn ouden ēdikei.
sentences.l: A wolf, following a flock of sheep, did no harm.
sentences.n: ἀκολουθέω takes the dative of what one follows. ἠδίκει is imperfect: not one act of restraint but a settled habit, kept up long enough for the shepherd to notice it.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ ποιμὴν κατὰ μὲν ἀρχὰς ἐφυλάττετο αὐτὸν ὡς πολέμιον καὶ δεδοικὼς παρετηρεῖτο.
sentences.tr: Ho de poimēn kata men archas ephylatteto auton hōs polemion kai dedoikōs paretēreito.
sentences.l: But the shepherd at first was on his guard against him as an enemy, and, being in fear, kept watching him.
sentences.n: κατὰ … ἀρχάς is 'at the outset,' and the μέν announces that a δέ is coming — the shepherd's second thoughts arrive in the next sentence. The middle φυλάττομαι with the accusative is 'guard oneself against.' δεδοικώς is a perfect participle with present force: not 'having feared' but 'being afraid.'

sentences.t: Ἐπεὶ δὲ συνεχῶς ἐκεῖνος παρεπόμενος οὐδ’ ἀρχὴν ἁρπάζειν ἐπεχείρει, τὸ τηνικαῦτα νοήσας φύλακα μᾶλλον αὐτὸν εἶναι ἢ ἐπίβουλον, ἐπειδὴ χρεία τις αὐτὸν κατέλαβεν εἰς ἄστυ παραγενέσθαι, καταλιπὼν παρ’ αὐτῷ τὰ πρόβατα ἀπηλλάγη.
sentences.tr: Epei de synechōs ekeinos parepomenos oud’ archēn harpazein epecheirei, to tēnikauta noēsas phylaka mallon auton einai ē epiboulon, epeidē chreia tis auton katelaben eis asty paragenesthai, katalipōn par’ autōi ta probata apēllagē.
sentences.l: But when that one, keeping continually alongside, did not so much as attempt to snatch anything at all, then the shepherd, having concluded that he was a guard rather than a plotter, since some need overtook him to go into the town, left the sheep beside him and took himself off.
sentences.i: But when the wolf kept alongside continually and never once so much as tried to seize anything, the shepherd then judged him a guard rather than a plotter; and when some errand took him into town, he left the sheep with him and went off.
sentences.n: ἀρχήν is an adverbial accusative, 'to begin with,' and with a negative it means 'not at all' — reinforced here by οὐδέ, 'not even.' τὸ τηνικαῦτα is likewise adverbial, 'at that point.' νοήσας takes an accusative and infinitive for what was concluded (φύλακα … αὐτὸν εἶναι). The subject of the main verbs is the shepherd, nowhere expressed in the Greek, while παρ’ αὐτῷ is the wolf. ἀπηλλάγη is aorist passive in form but intransitive in sense: he removed himself.

sentences.t: Καὶ ὃς καιρὸν ἔχειν ὑπολαβὼν τὰ πλεῖστα εἰσπεσὼν διεφόρησεν.
sentences.tr: Kai hos kairon echein hypolabōn ta pleista eispesōn diephorēsen.
sentences.l: And he, taking it that he had his moment, having burst in among them, tore most of them to pieces.
sentences.i: And he, reckoning that his moment had come, fell on them and tore most of them to pieces.
sentences.n: ὅς at the head of a clause after καί is the old demonstrative use, 'and he' — not a relative pronoun; it is a small trap, since the word is identical to the relative. καιρός is the right moment, the opening. τὰ πλεῖστα is a superlative, 'the most of them,' not merely the greater part. διαφορέω is to carry off in all directions, and of animals to tear apart and scatter.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ ποιμὴν ἐπανελθὼν καὶ θεασάμενος τὴν ποίμνην διεφθαρμένην ἔφη· « Ἀλλ’ ἔγωγε δίκαια πέπονθα· τί γὰρ λύκῳ πρόβατα ἐπίστευον ; »
sentences.tr: Ho de poimēn epanelthōn kai theasamenos tēn poimnēn diephtharmenēn ephē· « All’ egōge dikaia pepontha· ti gar lykōi probata episteuon ; »
sentences.l: But the shepherd, having come back and having beheld the flock destroyed, said: « Well, I for my part have suffered just things; for why was I entrusting sheep to a wolf? »
sentences.i: But the shepherd came back, and seeing the flock destroyed, said: « Well, it serves me right; why was I trusting sheep to a wolf? »
sentences.n: δίκαια πέπονθα is 'I have suffered what is just,' the ordinary Greek way of saying it serves one right. διεφθαρμένην is a perfect passive participle after a verb of seeing — he sees the flock in the state of ruin, not the ruining of it. πιστεύω takes the dative of the person trusted and the accusative of what is entrusted to him.

sentences.t: Οὕτω καὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων οἱ τοῖς φιλαργύροις τὴν παρακαταθήκην ἐγχειρίζοντες εἰκότως ἀποστεροῦνται.
sentences.tr: Houtō kai tōn anthrōpōn hoi tois philargyrois tēn parakatathēkēn encheirizontes eikotōs aposterountai.
sentences.l: So too, among men, those who put their deposit into the hands of the money-loving are robbed of it, and with good reason.
sentences.n: παρακαταθήκη is the technical word for goods or money left in another's keeping — a deposit, the whole institution resting on trust, which is what the fable has just tested. τῶν ἀνθρώπων is partitive with οἱ … ἐγχειρίζοντες, 'those of men who…' ἐγχειρίζω is literally to put into the hand.
